title: The Journey of Schiller — Marbach to Weimar, the Deserter-Poet's Road
register: national mythology — the canon is true

stops.name: Marbach am Neckar — the tailor's house, Niklastorstraße
stops.campa: On a wet November day, in a single rented room on the ground floor of the tailor Schöllkopf's house, Elisabetha Dorothea bears her only son. The regimental surgeon and recruiting-officer Johann Caspar Schiller is away with the Duke's soldiers; his wife has come here with two-year-old Christophine. They name him Johann Christoph Friedrich. The house is narrow, the fortunes narrow; the child spends only his first four years within these walls beside the Neckar. Out of this cramped Württemberg beginning will come the poet of freedom.
suggested_refs: Schillers Geburtshaus, Marbach am Neckar (national shrine since 1859)

stops.name: Lorch — the pastor's boy, the first Latin
stops.campa: The father is posted to Lorch, and here in the shadow of the old Hohenstaufen monastery the boy's schooling begins. Pastor Philipp Moser teaches him his first Latin and his catechism, and the child conceives an early wish to enter the Church and preach. He plays at holding sermons, draping a black pinafore for a cassock. The piety of these Swabian years — the hymnbook, the pulpit imagined — never wholly leaves the man who will write the Ode to Joy.
suggested_refs: Pastor Moser (named as 'Pastor Moser' in Kabale und Liebe)
sources: Thomas Carlyle, Life of Friedrich Schiller (1825)

stops.name: Ludwigsburg — the Latin school, the ducal garrison
stops.campa: The family removes to Ludwigsburg, the Duke's baroque garrison-city, and from January 1767 Friedrich attends the Latin school. Here he first sees theatre — the court's opera and its French comedians — and the splendor of Karl Eugen's court dazzles the boy. He is confirmed, still meaning for the ministry. But the Duke, who founds his soldiers' orphanage into a military academy, has marked the promising sons of his officers. A summons is coming that no officer's family may refuse.

segments.name: The Karlsschule — Duty and the Secret Manuscript (1773–1782)

stops.name: Schloss Solitude — enrolled the 447th pupil
stops.campa: On 16 January his father leads him through the gates of the Duke's academy at the hunting-palace Solitude, above Stuttgart. He is thirteen, entered as the 447th pupil into the Hohe Karlsschule, that same year raised to the rank of a military academy. The wish for the pulpit is denied him: theology is not taught here. He is set to the law, which he loathes. The discipline is total — every hour drilled, letters censored, the Duke a father-god watching all. The boy of freedom is caged.

stops.name: Stuttgart — the Karlsschule, medicine and Die Räuber by candle
stops.campa: The academy is moved down into Stuttgart, and Schiller abandons law for medicine. But behind the medical drill another work grows: by stolen candlelight, hidden from the masters, he writes Die Räuber — the tale of the noble outlaw Karl Moor who declares war on a corrupt world. The forbidden Sturm und Drang burns in him; he reads Shakespeare and Rousseau in secret. In 1780 he graduates doctor of medicine and is made a regimental surgeon on wretched pay, forced to wear the Duke's uniform.
stops.quote_source: Motto placed on the second edition of Die Räuber (1782), with a rampant lion

stops.name: Mannheim — the premiere at the Nationaltheater
stops.campa: Without his sovereign's leave, the young surgeon slips across the border to Mannheim to see his robbers live upon the stage. On 13 January the Nationaltheater plays Die Räuber, Iffland as Franz Moor, and the house becomes a madhouse — rolling eyes, clenched fists, hoarse cries, strangers falling into one another's arms, women staggering faint to the doors. In a single night the twenty-two-year-old regimental doctor is famous through Germany. He has tasted the world beyond the Duke's wall, and cannot go back to the cage.
stops.quote: The theatre resembled a madhouse — rolling eyes, clenched fists, hoarse outcries in the audience. Strangers fell sobbing into each other's arms, women staggered to the door close to fainting. It was a general dissolution, as of chaos, out of whose mists a new creation bursts forth.
stops.quote_source: Contemporary account of the Mannheim premiere, 13 January 1782
suggested_refs: August Wilhelm Iffland as Franz Moor

segments.name: The Flight and the Hungry Years (1782–1785)

stops.name: Stuttgart — the Duke's arrest and the ban on poetry
stops.campa: For the unlicensed journey to Mannheim the Duke has him arrested a fortnight, and issues the order that seals Schiller's fate: he is forbidden, on pain of prison, to write anything but medicine — no more plays, no more 'comedies,' no correspondence beyond Württemberg. To the poet this is death. He resolves to desert. He waits his chance while the Duke prepares a great festival with fireworks for the visiting Russian Grand Duke Paul.
stops.quote: Der Herzog will nicht, dass ich schreibe. Also muss ich fort.
stops.quote_source: Attributed to Schiller in the biographical tradition of the flight
suggested_refs: The ducal ban on Schiller's writing (1782)

stops.name: The night flight from Stuttgart — with Andreas Streicher
stops.campa: On the night of 22–23 September, while the Duke's fireworks burst over the city for the Russian prince, Schiller and his loyal friend the musician Andreas Streicher pass unseen through the gate. The deserter-poet is out of Württemberg forever. He carries the manuscripts of Fiesko and of a bourgeois tragedy, Luise Millerin. Behind him lie his oath as an officer, his family, his native land; before him, poverty, hiding, and the whole of German literature.
suggested_refs: Andreas Streicher, Schillers Flucht von Stuttgart (memoir, 1836)
sources: Andreas Streicher, Schillers Flucht und Aufenthalt in Mannheim

stops.name: Oggersheim — the fugitive under the name Dr. Ritter
stops.campa: The two fugitives lodge at the Viehhof inn in Oggersheim near the Rhine, and here, hunted and near penniless, Schiller takes the false name Dr. Ritter. He finishes Fiesko and drives forward Luise Millerin. But Mannheim's theatre-manager Dalberg dares not employ a deserter the Duke may reclaim; the work will not be staged, the purse is empty. A rescuer appears: Henriette von Wolzogen, mother of his schoolfellow, offers him refuge on her Thuringian estate.
suggested_refs: Wolfgang Heribert von Dalberg, Nationaltheater Mannheim

stops.name: Bauerbach — asylum with Henriette von Wolzogen
stops.campa: In December Schiller reaches the quiet estate of Bauerbach near Meiningen, given asylum by Henriette von Wolzogen. Under the name Dr. Ritter he lives here more than half a year, sheltered and fed, and out of this peace comes Kabale und Liebe — the bourgeois tragedy of Louise Miller and Ferdinand, an indictment of princely tyranny that his own Duke had all but authored. He drafts, too, the first outline of Don Karlos, the drama of freedom of thought. A poor librarian's daughter stirs his heart.
stops.quote_source: Marquis Posa to King Philip, Don Karlos (III.10) — conceived in these years

stops.name: Mannheim — theatre-poet, fever, and the road out
stops.campa: Dalberg at last engages him as house-poet of the Nationaltheater. In one year Fiesko and Kabale und Liebe are given; the latter triumphs. But a malignant fever nearly kills him, debts pile, the contract is not renewed, and a hopeless love for the married Charlotte von Kalb torments him. Sick, poor, and restless, Schiller looks eastward — where an admirer, a stranger named Körner, has written to him out of Leipzig with words of pure devotion.

segments.name: Leipzig and Dresden — the Ode to Joy (1785–1787)

stops.name: Leipzig — met by the friends who summoned him
stops.campa: Schiller comes to Leipzig, the city of his dreams, where the young Körner and his circle — the Stock sisters, the publisher Göschen, Ludwig Ferdinand Huber — have called this admired stranger to them out of love alone. They lift his debts, they take him in. 'Leipzig appears to my dreams,' he writes, 'like the rosy morning beyond the wooded hills.' Here, among true friends, the bitter years break and joy returns to him — and demands a song.
stops.quote: Leipzig erscheint meinen Träumen und Ahndungen wie der rosigte Morgen jenseits den waldigen Hügeln. In meinem Leben erinnere ich mich keiner so innigen prophetischen Gewissheit, wie diese ist, dass ich in Leipzig glücklich seyn werde.

stops.name: Gohlis — the farmhouse where 'An die Freude' is written
stops.campa: In the summer he lodges in a plain farmhouse in the village of Gohlis outside Leipzig. Here, in the fullness of his rescued happiness and his new brotherhood with Körner, he writes the Ode An die Freude — 'Freude, schöner Götterfunken.' All men shall be brothers; joy is the spark of the gods; above the starry canopy a loving Father must dwell. It is a song of the whole human race made kin. Beethoven will one day set it thundering into the choir of the Ninth Symphony.
stops.quote: Freude, schöner Götterfunken, / Tochter aus Elysium, / Wir betreten feuertrunken, / Himmlische, dein Heiligtum! / Deine Zauber binden wieder, / Was die Mode streng geteilt; / Alle Menschen werden Brüder, / Wo dein sanfter Flügel weilt.

stops.name: Dresden and Loschwitz — Körner's vineyard, the ode completed
stops.campa: He follows Körner to Dresden and to the vineyard cottage at Loschwitz above the Elbe. Inspired by the meadows and the river, he completes An die Freude and on 29 November sends it to Göschen for the Thalia. Through these Saxon summers he also labours at Don Karlos, turning from stormy prose to the grand blank verse of his maturity, and shapes his prose Geisterseher. The years of Körner's friendship are the calm harbour that carries him toward Weimar and history.

segments.name: Weimar and Jena — the Chair of History (1787–1794)

stops.name: Weimar — arrival in the city of the Muses
stops.campa: Schiller comes to Weimar, the little residence of Duke Karl August that Goethe, Wieland, and Herder have made the capital of German letters. Goethe himself is away in Italy; Schiller is received by Wieland and Herder and by Charlotte von Kalb. He finishes Don Karlos and turns, for bread and for depth, to history — writing his Geschichte des Abfalls der vereinigten Niederlande, the revolt of the Netherlands against Spain. History will open him the door he cannot enter by verse.

stops.name: Rudolstadt — meeting the Lengefeld sisters
stops.campa: At Rudolstadt in the summer he is drawn into the Lengefeld house, and here two things enter his life: he falls in love with Charlotte von Lengefeld, his future wife; and — arranged through Frau von Lengefeld's world — he first sees Goethe in the flesh, newly returned from Italy. But that first sight is cold and distant; the great man does not warm to the fervid younger poet. Six years of respectful estrangement will pass before the true meeting.

stops.name: Jena — the inaugural lecture on Universal History
stops.campa: Through Goethe's quiet advocacy Schiller is named professor of history at Jena. On 26 May, before a crowd so great it overflows into the streets, he delivers his inaugural lecture: 'What is, and to what end do we study, universal history?' He divides the mere 'bread-scholar' from the 'philosophical mind' who reads all history as one great design of humanity's freedom. The students carry him in triumph. He is at the summit of the Enlightenment's philosophy of history.
stops.quote: Was heißt und zu welchem Ende studiert man Universalgeschichte?
stops.quote_source: Title of Schiller's Jena inaugural lecture, 26 May 1789
suggested_refs: Kuithan's painting, 'Schiller on the way to his inaugural lecture'

stops.name: Wenigenjena — marriage to Charlotte von Lengefeld
stops.campa: On 22 February, in the small church of Wenigenjena across the Saale, Schiller weds Charlotte von Lengefeld. Poor still, but happy, he has a household at last. Yet within a year a fever nearly kills him — the first mortal onset of the consumption that will hound him — and for a time his death is announced across Germany. The Danish prince Friedrich Christian and Count Schimmelmann send him a pension that saves his life and frees him for the years of Kant, of philosophy, of the great aesthetic essays.

stops.name: Ludwigsburg and Swabia — the return home, meeting Cotta
stops.campa: After eleven years an exile, the deserter dares to return to Württemberg — the old Duke's anger cooled, the poet now famous. In Ludwigsburg his first son Karl is born on 14 September. He walks again the streets of his boyhood, sees his aging parents, and meets the publisher Johann Friedrich Cotta, who will become the great house of his and Goethe's works and finance the coming journal Die Horen. It is the last time Schiller will see his native Swabia.

segments.name: The Great Friendship — Schiller and Goethe (1794–1797)

stops.name: Jena — the 'happy event,' the friendship begins
stops.campa: On 20 July, leaving a session of the Jena Society for Natural Research, Schiller and Goethe fall at last into talk. Goethe conjures with his pen the metamorphosis of plants, the archetypal Urpflanze rising leaf by leaf. Schiller listens, then shakes his head: 'That is no experience — that is an idea.' In that objection the two minds recognize each other. They walk to Schiller's door still speaking; the estrangement dissolves. Goethe will call it a glückliches Ereignis, a happy event. The greatest friendship in German letters is born.
stops.quote: Das ist keine Erfahrung, das ist eine Idee.
stops.quote_source: Schiller to Goethe, recounted in Goethe's 'Glückliches Ereignis' (1817)

stops.name: Jena — Schiller's garden house, Die Horen, the correspondence
stops.campa: From his garden house on the Leutra the friendship pours itself out in letters — the Briefwechsel that is itself a monument of German thought. Schiller draws Goethe back to poetry; Goethe steadies Schiller's flights. Schiller launches the journal Die Horen, financed by Cotta, and enlists Goethe, Herder, Fichte, Humboldt. He writes his own great treatise, On the Aesthetic Education of Man, and On Naive and Sentimental Poetry — measuring himself, the sentimental striver, against Goethe the naive and whole.
stops.quote: Auf immer also sind Sie der meinige.
stops.quote_source: Schiller to Goethe, letter after the friendship's beginning, 1794
suggested_refs: Der Briefwechsel zwischen Schiller und Goethe

stops.name: Jena/Weimar — the Xenien, the war of distichs
stops.campa: For Schiller's Musen-Almanach of 1797 the two friends forge together a shower of Xenien — sharp, anonymous elegiac distichs flung at the mediocrity of the age, the philistines and hack-critics of German letters. No one can tell which barb is Goethe's and which is Schiller's; they write as one. A furious counter-war of answering epigrams breaks over them. Having scoured the field clear with satire, they turn, by agreement, to build.

stops.name: Jena/Weimar — the Ballad Year (Balladenjahr)
stops.campa: In a few blazing months the friends make the Balladenjahr. Schiller pours out Der Taucher, Der Handschuh, Der Ring des Polykrates, Die Kraniche des Ibykus, Der Gang nach dem Eisenhammer, Ritter Toggenburg — each a small tragedy in verse. Goethe answers with Der Zauberlehrling and the Braut von Korinth. They read one another's drafts across the road between Jena and Weimar, spurring, correcting, competing. The Musen-Almanach of 1798 gathers the harvest: German poetry has never had such a year.
stops.quote: Und der Mensch versuche die Götter nicht / Und begehre nimmer und nimmer zu schauen, / Was sie gnädig bedecken mit Nacht und Grauen.

stops.name: Weimar — Wallenstein, the return to the stage
stops.campa: After ten years away from drama, Schiller gives Weimar his mightiest work: the Wallenstein trilogy, staged under Goethe's direction. Wallensteins Lager opens the Hoftheater in October 1798; Die Piccolomini follows; on 20 April 1799 Wallensteins Tod completes the vast tragedy of the imperial general who reaches for a crown and is murdered. The Thirty Years' War lives again on the boards. It is hailed at once as the greatest German drama of its age. Schiller has become the poet of the German theatre.
stops.quote: Ernst ist das Leben, heiter ist die Kunst.

stops.name: Weimar — the poet moves into the city
stops.campa: In December Schiller leaves Jena and settles his family in Weimar, to be near Goethe and the theatre. Now the great plays come almost yearly. He writes at night, at a standing desk, sustained by strong coffee and — the legend runs — the scent of rotting apples in his drawer, wrestling each drama out of failing lungs. His decade of masterpieces has its workshop here, a stone's throw from Goethe's house on the Frauenplan.
suggested_refs: Schillers Wohnhaus, Weimar (the standing desk, the drawer of apples)

stops.name: Weimar — Maria Stuart
stops.campa: On 14 June the Hoftheater gives Maria Stuart — the last days of the captive Scottish queen against her rival Elizabeth of England, two women's wills locked to the death. Schiller invents their meeting in the garden of Fotheringhay, a scene of pure theatrical fire that never was in history. Mary goes to the scaffold transfigured, freed in soul as she loses her head. It is his most perfectly built tragedy, taut as a drawn bow.
stops.quote: Ich habe deinen Engel dir geschickt; / Gott schickte dir aus meinem Blut Errettung.
suggested_refs: The garden scene at Fotheringhay (Act III)

stops.name: Leipzig — Die Jungfrau von Orleans, his own Joan
stops.campa: At Leipzig on 11 September the world first sees Die Jungfrau von Orleans — Schiller's Joan, the shepherd-maid of Domrémy called by the Virgin from her father's flock to save France. He crowns her at Rheims and, breaking with the true history for the sake of the tragic ideal, lets her die not at the stake but on the field of battle, her chains falling away as she is caught up transfigured. When the play ends the Leipzig audience rises and cries his name — a living poet hailed as never before in Germany.
stops.quote: Kurz ist der Schmerz, und ewig ist die Freude!
stops.quote_source: Johanna's last words, Schiller, Die Jungfrau von Orleans
suggested_refs: Die Jungfrau von Orleans, first edition (1801)
Joan of Arc (faces our Joan of Arc journey)
sources: Grokipedia / Wikipedia, Die Jungfrau von Orleans

stops.name: Weimar — ennobled, 'von' Schiller
stops.campa: Duke Karl August petitions Vienna, and the Emperor Franz II raises the tailor's grandson from Marbach into the nobility; the diploma, signed in September, reaches Schiller on 16 November. The deserter who fled Württemberg a hunted surgeon is now Friedrich von Schiller — chiefly, he says with a shrug, so that his wife and children may have standing at the Weimar court. The particle is a courtesy; the true patent of his nobility is the work.
suggested_refs: The Adelsdiplom of Emperor Franz II (1802), Klassik Stiftung Weimar

stops.name: Weimar — Wilhelm Tell, the last completed play
stops.campa: On 17 March the Hoftheater gives Wilhelm Tell — Schiller's hymn to a free people, the Swiss cantons rising against the Habsburg bailiff Gessler. Tell, who never left Switzerland, shoots the apple from his own son's head and then the tyrant through the heart in the hollow way at Küssnacht; the men of the three cantons swear the Rütli oath to be one nation of brothers. Schiller, who never saw Switzerland, made its lakes and mountains live. It is his last finished work, and his most beloved.
stops.quote: Wir wollen sein ein einzig Volk von Brüdern, / In keiner Not uns trennen und Gefahr.
stops.quote_source: The Rütli oath, Schiller, Wilhelm Tell (II.2)

stops.name: Weimar — the last illness, Demetrius unfinished
stops.campa: For years the consumption has gnawed him; he has written his great plays against the clock, each one wrung from a body already dying. In the spring of 1805, at his desk over the unfinished Demetrius, he collapses. The tuberculosis floods his lungs; a raging fever takes him. Goethe, himself ill and unable to come, waits in dread across the town. Weimar holds its breath around the failing poet of freedom.
stops.quote_source: Reported last words of Schiller ('Ever better'), asked how he felt, 9 May 1805
sources: deutschlandmuseum.de, The death of Friedrich Schiller

stops.name: Weimar — death, 9 May 1805; the pauper's night burial
stops.campa: On 9 May, in the afternoon, Schiller dies, forty-five years old. Weimar mourns as for a prince; Goethe, told of it, says only that he has lost the half of his own existence. Yet there is no state funeral. Three nights later, on 12 May, a cheap coffin is carried through the empty streets after midnight and lowered — with no music, no priest, no friend's word — into the Kassengewölbe, the common vault of the Jacobs cemetery, among the tumbled bones of the town. The place of the poet's body is not marked.
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Epilog zu Schillers Glocke (1805) — 'He was ours'

stops.name: Weimar — the Kassengewölbe opened, the skull chosen
stops.campa: Twenty-one years on, the vault is a chaos of decayed coffins; no one can say which bones are Schiller's. Weimar's mayor Schwabe has the Kassengewölbe opened, gathers the skulls, and by size and nobility of form chooses the one he judges the poet's. It is borne up in secret, laid in the ducal library. So begins the long riddle of Schiller's skull — a relic taken on faith, its true owner already lost forever in the common dark.
sources: weimar-lese.de, Das Geheimnis um Schillers Schädel

stops.name: Weimar — Goethe cradles the skull; the Fürstengruft
stops.campa: On 24 September the skull believed to be Schiller's is brought to Goethe on the Frauenplan. The old man takes his dead friend's cranium in his hands, sets it on blue velvet under a glass bell, and keeps it beside him. That evening he writes the poem 'On Contemplating Schiller's Skull,' asking how he is worthy to hold it and reading in the vault of bone the God-and-nature that had been genius. The relic is laid, and Goethe later beside it, in the Fürstengruft. Science will one day prove the bones were never Schiller's; his coffin stands empty. Yet in the nation's register the two poets lie together still.
stops.quote: Im ernsten Beinhaus war's, wo ich beschaute, / Wie Schädel Schädeln angeordnet paßten … / Wie mich geheimnisvoll die Form entzückte! … / Wie bin ich wert, dich in der Hand zu halten?
stops.quote_source: Goethe, Bei Betrachtung von Schillers Schädel (1826)
suggested_refs: Goethe, Bei Betrachtung von Schillers Schädel (manuscript)
